lessons.title: Why indemnification is the hardest part of a deal to picture

blocks.markdown:
Most people who negotiate indemnification clauses have never watched one operate.

That is not a criticism. It is structural. Claims are rare relative to deals. A dealmaker might close twenty agreements and see a single third-party claim arise from any of them. And when that claim does arrive, it usually lands on a different desk. Litigation counsel takes the file. The person who negotiated the cap three years earlier rarely learns whether the number they fought for mattered.

The result is a strange asymmetry. Indemnity language is among the most heavily negotiated parts of an agreement, and among the parts whose real-world operation is least understood by the people negotiating it.

Reading an indemnification clause tells you what it says. It does not tell you what happens in month seven, when the claim is live, the parties disagree about whether to settle, and the insurer has just sent a reservation of rights letter.

## The spine of this module

This module is built around that gap. Its spine is the third-party claim lifecycle: a letter arrives, notice gets given, someone takes control of the defense, the parties argue about settlement, and eventually money moves — or doesn't.

Everything else you will meet here — representations, warranties, caps, baskets, survival periods, escrow, insurance — is taught as machinery that determines how that lifecycle plays out.

That reframing matters more than it might sound.

A cap is not an abstract number. It is the point at which the indemnifying party stops caring about the outcome of a litigation they may still be controlling. A survival period is not a date. It is the moment a problem you have not yet discovered becomes permanently yours. A consent-to-settle provision is not a formality. It is the mechanism that decides who wins an argument the parties are certain to have.

## One thing worth naming early

A large part of indemnity negotiation is not really about indemnity. It is about price.

When a buyer pushes the cap from ten per cent of deal value to twenty, they are buying something. The seller is selling it. The parties are allocating residual risk, and residual risk has a value that could in principle be reflected in the headline number instead.

Treating the negotiation as a purely legal argument, rather than a commercial one with legal vocabulary, is a common way to lose it.

## What this module does not do

It does not teach you to draft. It does not substitute for counsel — and where a point turns on the law of a particular jurisdiction, that will be said plainly rather than buried.

What it should do is let you sit in a negotiation, or in the first meeting after a claim letter arrives, and understand what the package in front of you actually does under stress.

options: Indemnity clauses are rarely enforced in commercial practice

lessons.title: Representations and warranties: the foundation indemnity sits on

blocks.markdown:
Almost every indemnification claim begins in the same place: someone said something that turned out not to be true.

That makes representations and warranties the foundation the whole indemnity package rests on. Understanding what they are — and more importantly, what qualifies them — determines how much protection the indemnity actually provides.

## Three words that are not interchangeable

A **representation** is a statement of fact about the present or the past. The seller represents that it owns the assets, that the regulatory filings are accurate, that there is no pending litigation beyond what has been disclosed.

A **warranty** is a promise that the statement is true, carrying a remedy if it is not.

A **covenant** is different in kind: a promise to do, or refrain from doing, something going forward. Operating the business in the ordinary course between signing and closing is a covenant, not a representation.

In practice, commercial agreements bundle the first two into a single formula — *represents and warrants* — and in most civil law jurisdictions the distinction carries little practical consequence.

Under English and US law it historically mattered. A false representation could support rescission or a claim in tort; a breached warranty gave contract damages. The combined formula survives partly out of caution and partly out of habit. It is worth knowing that the two words are doing different historical work, even where a court will treat them as one.

## Two words that can gut a representation

*To the seller's knowledge.*

A knowledge qualifier converts a promise that something is true into a promise that the seller is not aware it is false. Everything the seller genuinely did not know becomes the buyer's problem.

This is not a drafting nicety. It is one of the largest risk transfers available in a commercial agreement, and it is accomplished in four words.

Three questions decide how much a knowledge qualifier costs:

- **Whose knowledge counts?** The company's? Named individuals'? Anyone in management?
- **Actual or constructive?** Does it mean what the seller genuinely knew, or also what a reasonable enquiry would have surfaced?
- **Is it defined at all?** An unqualified reference to "knowledge" with no definition is an invitation to argue about it later, at a point when both sides have strong incentives to remember things differently.

A defined knowledge standard naming specific individuals and specifying actual versus constructive awareness is worth more than an extra few percentage points on the cap.

## Materiality, and scraping it out

*In all material respects* does similar work from a different angle. It excuses small inaccuracies, and shifts the argument to whether a given inaccuracy was small.

Which is why the **materiality scrape** exists. A scrape instructs the reader to ignore materiality qualifiers when calculating losses — so once a breach is established, damages are measured on the full amount rather than only the portion above the materiality line.

A **double materiality scrape** goes further and removes materiality for determining whether a breach occurred at all, not merely for quantifying it. The difference between the two is frequently glossed over in negotiation and is not small.

## Where a great deal of real risk allocation actually happens

Then there are the disclosure schedules.

Anything properly disclosed against a representation is carved out of it. The seller is not in breach of a representation about pending litigation for the litigation it listed. Schedules are, in substance, a second negotiation about risk — conducted in a spreadsheet.

They are also usually assembled late, under time pressure, and with less senior attention than the clause language received. A sophisticated buyer reads the schedules at least as carefully as the reps. Many do not.

cards.back: A statement of fact about the present or the past — that the assets are owned, the filings are accurate, the disclosed litigation is complete.
A promise that a statement is true, carrying a remedy if it is not. Usually bundled with representation as 'represents and warrants'.
A promise to do or not do something going forward — different in kind from a representation, which looks backward or at the present.
Language ('to the seller's knowledge') converting a promise that something is true into a promise that the seller is unaware it is false. Shifts unknown risk to the buyer.
A provision reading materiality qualifiers out when calculating losses. A double scrape also removes them when determining whether a breach occurred.

questions.stem: What is the practical effect of a knowledge qualifier on a representation?
options: It limits the amount recoverable for breach of that representation
It shortens the period during which the representation survives
It shifts the risk of matters the seller did not know about onto the buyer
It requires the buyer to conduct independent verification before closing
questions.explanation: A knowledge qualifier changes the promise from 'this is true' to 'I am not aware this is false'. Anything the seller genuinely did not know falls outside the representation and therefore outside the indemnity that rests on it.

blocks.markdown:
An indemnification regime answers six questions. They are worth separating, because they are negotiated on different logic and they fail in different ways.

- Who indemnifies whom
- For what losses
- Triggered by what
- Subject to what procedure
- Limited how
- To the exclusion of what other remedies

Most of this module deals with the fourth and fifth. This lesson covers the rest.

## Indemnify, defend, hold harmless

These three appear together so often that they read as a single incantation. They are not the same thing.

**Indemnify** means reimburse for losses suffered. It operates after the fact.

**Defend** is an obligation that arises earlier and is often broader: a duty to take on and fund the defense of a claim from the moment it is asserted, regardless of whether it eventually proves meritorious. A party can owe a defense on a claim it ultimately owes no indemnity on — the claim fails, but the defense still had to be paid for while it was live.

**Hold harmless** is treated by many courts as synonymous with indemnify. It is sometimes argued to be broader: protection from liability arising at all, rather than reimbursement once it has. The argument is worth knowing even where a court collapses the two.

attributes.label: When it arises
values: After liability is established — reimburses losses already suffered
When the claim is asserted, not when it is proven
Often treated as synonymous with indemnify; sometimes argued to prevent liability arising at all

attributes.label: Owed even if claim fails?
values: No — owed only where the indemnity is actually triggered
Yes — defense costs accrue while the claim is live regardless of outcome
Depends on how the court reads it; worth reading carefully rather than assuming it is filler

blocks.markdown:
## What counts as a loss

The definition of covered losses is where a surprising amount of value sits, and it is often skimmed because it looks like boilerplate.

Does it include legal fees and the costs of investigation? Fees incurred in pursuing the indemnity claim itself, as opposed to defending the underlying claim? Amounts paid in settlement, and if so, settlements entered into without the indemnifying party's consent? Diminution in value of the acquired business, or only out-of-pocket amounts?

Each of these is a live negotiation point dressed as a definition.

## Triggers

Most indemnities are triggered by one of three things: breach of a representation or warranty, breach of a covenant, or a specifically identified matter.

The first is the most common and is the reason the previous lesson spent its time on qualifiers. The second is usually less contested. The third deserves its own paragraph.

## Specific indemnities

Some risks are known to both parties at signing. Litigation already filed. A regulatory question already under discussion with an agency. A recall in progress. An environmental liability at a manufacturing site.

These are commonly pulled out of the general regime and given their own indemnity — and they typically sit outside the cap, outside the basket, and sometimes outside the survival period.

The logic is clean once stated. The general regime allocates *unknown* risk, and its limits are priced accordingly. A specific indemnity allocates a risk both parties can name and size. There is no reason to make a known liability compete with unknown ones for room under a shared cap.

## Exclusive remedy

Most well-constructed indemnity regimes include an exclusive remedy provision: indemnification is the sole recourse for breaches of the agreement, to the exclusion of other contractual or tortious claims.

Without it, the carefully negotiated caps, baskets and survival periods can be circumvented by pleading the same facts as misrepresentation or negligence and escaping the limits entirely.

The carve-out is almost always fraud. The scope of that carve-out repays careful reading, because 'fraud' can be defined narrowly enough to be nearly unreachable, or broadly enough to swallow the exclusivity it is carved out of.

cards.back: Indemnify reimburses losses after the fact. Defend funds the defense from the moment a claim is asserted — and can be owed on claims that ultimately fail.
An indemnity for a known, identified risk (pending litigation, a live regulatory issue). Usually sits outside the cap, basket and sometimes the survival period.
Makes indemnification the sole recourse for breach, preventing the negotiated limits from being circumvented by tort or misrepresentation claims. Almost always carves out fraud.

questions.stem: Why do specific indemnities typically sit outside the general cap and basket?
options: Because they are usually smaller than general indemnity claims
Because the general regime prices unknown risk, while a specific indemnity covers a risk both parties can already name and size
Because they are governed by different law than the rest of the agreement
Because insurers require known liabilities to be separately stated
questions.explanation: The general regime's limits are calibrated to unknown risk. A liability both parties can identify and quantify at signing has no reason to compete for room under a cap priced for uncertainty.

lessons.title: Direct claims and third-party claims: two different machines

blocks.markdown:
There are two fundamentally different ways an indemnity gets called on, and agreements routinely blur them.

A **direct claim** is one party to the agreement claiming against the other. The buyer discovers after closing that a representation was false, and claims against the seller. Nobody from outside is involved.

A **third-party claim** is an outside party — a patient, a regulator, a competitor, a tax authority — asserting a claim against the indemnified party, with the indemnifying party on the hook for the consequences.

## Why the procedures diverge sharply

In a direct claim there is nothing to defend. No external proceeding, no outside claimant, no real-time decisions. The procedure is simply: notice, a response period, and then whatever dispute resolution mechanism the agreement provides. The entire question is whether the indemnity is owed.

In a third-party claim there is a live proceeding that somebody has to run. Counsel must be instructed. Filings have deadlines. Settlement offers arrive and expire. Decisions must be made continuously, by someone, while the parties may disagree about what those decisions should be.

That is why the third-party machinery exists: notice requirements, control of defense, cooperation duties, consent to settle. None of it has any application to a direct claim.

values: No external proceeding to defend

blocks.markdown:
## Where agreements get this wrong

Three failure patterns show up repeatedly.

The first is a single combined procedure. The agreement defines "Claim" once and applies one set of mechanics to everything, producing provisions that make no sense when read against a direct claim. Who assumes the defense of a claim that has no defense?

The second is the opposite: elaborate third-party machinery and no direct claim procedure at all. The buyer discovers a breach and finds the agreement silent on how to assert it — what notice is required, what the seller's response window is, what happens if the seller simply does not reply.

The third is subtler. Direct claim notice requirements are often borrowed from the third-party section without adjustment, importing conditions that are natural for an external claim and difficult for an internal one.

## The notice trap in direct claims

This is where direct claims most often die.

A typical provision requires notice specifying the basis for the claim, the representation alleged to have been breached, and a good-faith estimate of the loss. That last requirement is the problem. A buyer can discover in month twenty that something is wrong, know it is a breach, and be genuinely unable to quantify it — because the investigation is ongoing, or because the loss depends on a regulatory outcome that will not arrive for another year.

If the survival period ends at month twenty-four, the buyer is forced to choose between a notice that may be attacked as deficient and no notice at all.

The practical answer, negotiated in advance, is language permitting notice of a claim with an estimate "to the extent then determinable," preserving the claim without demanding a number that does not yet exist.

## One set of facts, both claim types

The two are not mutually exclusive, and in pharma they frequently arrive together.

A patient brings a product liability claim against the acquired business. That is a third-party claim, and the third-party procedure governs how it is defended. But the fact that the seller knew of the safety signal and did not disclose it is also a breach of a representation — a direct claim, with its own notice requirement and its own path.

The same facts, two procedures, two sets of deadlines, and a real risk that satisfying one while overlooking the other leaves part of the exposure unrecovered.

cards.back: A claim by one party to the agreement against the other, with no outside claimant. No defense to control — the only question is whether the indemnity is owed.
A claim by an outside party against the indemnified party, with the indemnifying party on the hook. Requires real-time defense decisions, hence the procedural machinery.

questions.stem: Why do third-party claims require procedural provisions that direct claims do not?
options: Third-party claims are typically larger in value
A third-party claim involves a live external proceeding requiring continuous real-time decisions by someone
Direct claims are usually resolved before any procedure applies
Insurers only require notice for third-party claims
questions.explanation: A third-party claim means an outside proceeding that must actually be run — counsel instructed, deadlines met, settlement offers answered. Control, cooperation and consent-to-settle provisions exist to decide who makes those calls. A direct claim has no defense to conduct.

lessons.title: A third-party claim arrives: the first thirty days

blocks.markdown:
A letter arrives. A regulator opens an inquiry. A competitor files. Whatever the form, the clock has started, and several clocks have started at once.

The first weeks after a claim surfaces determine a surprising amount of what follows. Not because the legal merits change, but because the procedural and coverage positions can be permanently damaged in that window — quietly, by people acting reasonably.

blocks.markdown:
## What the notice provision actually requires

Read it for three things.

**Timing.** "Promptly," "as soon as reasonably practicable," or a specific number of days. The vaguer formulations are more forgiving in principle and more arguable in practice.

**Content.** A description of the claim, the basis on which indemnification is sought, copies of the claim documents, and often an estimate of the loss. Notice that omits a required element can be attacked as defective even when it arrived on time.

**Consequence.** This is the one people skip. Does the agreement say notice is a *condition precedent* to indemnification?

## The prejudice question

Under most commercial law, late notice defeats an indemnity claim only to the extent the indemnifying party was actually prejudiced by the delay. If they lost the ability to defend effectively, the argument bites. If they lost nothing, courts are generally reluctant to void the indemnity over a procedural slip.

That comfortable position weakens considerably where the agreement makes notice an express condition precedent. Then the failure is not a breach to be measured — it is an unmet condition, and the obligation may never arise at all.

The word to search for is *condition*. It changes the risk profile of a missed deadline from arguable to fatal.

## Two clocks, not one

Here is the failure that quietly destroys more value than any drafting error.

The contractual notice goes to the indemnifying party. A separate notice is owed to the insurer under the policy. They run on **different deadlines with different requirements**, and the insurance clock is the less forgiving of the two.

Late notice to a counterparty is usually met with the prejudice argument above. Late notice to an insurer can eliminate coverage outright. Under a **claims-made** policy, notice within the policy period is not merely a procedural step — it is what triggers coverage to exist at all.

The pattern is familiar and entirely avoidable: legal notifies the counterparty within the contractual window, the broker is told weeks later once the matter feels serious, and the policy that would have covered the loss is no longer available.

blocks.markdown:
## The litigation hold

One item on that list deserves separating out, because it is the one most often handled badly by people who have never done it.

When a claim becomes reasonably foreseeable, the duty to preserve relevant documents attaches. Routine deletion policies must be suspended for anything within scope. Custodians must be identified and instructed.

Get this wrong and the consequences are not confined to the underlying claim. Spoliation findings travel: adverse inferences, sanctions, and a defense conducted from a materially weaker position regardless of the merits. It is also the kind of failure that makes an indemnifying party genuinely prejudiced by your handling of the matter — which is precisely the argument that converts a technical notice defect into a real one.

## What not to do

Do not engage substantively with the claimant before internal alignment. A well-intentioned reply acknowledging facts, offering an explanation, or proposing a commercial resolution can prejudice the defense and complicate coverage before anyone with responsibility for either has seen the file.

And do not wait for certainty before notifying. Both the contractual and policy notice provisions are generally satisfied by notifying a claim that *may* give rise to liability. Waiting until the position is clear is how deadlines are missed.

cards.back: Language making notice a precondition to the indemnity obligation arising at all. Converts a missed deadline from an arguable breach into a potentially fatal failure.
A policy where notice within the policy period is what triggers coverage to exist. Late notice does not merely weaken the claim — it can eliminate coverage.
Suspension of routine document deletion once a claim becomes reasonably foreseeable. Failure can produce spoliation sanctions independent of the claim's merits.

questions.stem: Why is late notice to an insurer generally more damaging than late notice to the indemnifying party?
options: Insurance policies carry statutory notice deadlines that contracts cannot vary
Insurers are not subject to the prejudice analysis that usually softens late contractual notice, and under a claims-made policy timely notice is what creates coverage at all
Contractual notice deadlines are generally longer than policy deadlines
Insurers cannot decline coverage once a claim has been asserted
questions.explanation: Late contractual notice is usually measured against actual prejudice to the indemnifying party. Policy notice is treated far more strictly, and with a claims-made policy notice inside the period is the event that brings coverage into existence.

lessons.title: Control of defense: who runs the litigation

blocks.markdown:
Control of defense is the most consequential procedural term in an indemnity package and the one least likely to be argued about at signing.

It decides who selects counsel, who sets strategy, who decides what to concede, and whose judgment governs when a settlement offer lands. It determines, in practice, whether the litigation is run to minimise payout or run to protect a business.

## Why each side wants it

The **indemnifying party** wants control because they are paying. Their concern is straightforward and legitimate: a party defending a claim with someone else's money has weak incentives to defend economically. Every hour of senior counsel, every expert retained, every motion filed is billed to a payer with no say.

The **indemnified party** resists because the claim is happening to their business. They still sell the product. They still have the regulatory relationship. They will still be operating in that market long after the file closes.

A defense optimised to minimise a payment is not the same defense as one optimised to protect a franchise. A settlement carrying an admission, or a public filing making a damaging concession on a scientific point, may be an excellent outcome for the payer and a serious problem for the operator.

## The mechanics

Most regimes follow the same shape.

Following notice, the indemnifying party has a defined window — commonly fifteen to thirty days — to **elect to assume the defense**. Silence is usually treated as declining.

If they assume it, counsel is typically required to be *reasonably satisfactory to* the indemnified party. That phrase is doing real work and is worth negotiating rather than accepting as boilerplate.

The indemnified party normally retains a right to **participate at its own expense** — to have its own counsel monitor, attend, and be consulted, without controlling.

If the indemnifying party declines or fails to elect, the indemnified party defends, and can generally recover reasonable defense costs as part of the indemnified loss.

## The carve-outs that shift control back

A well-drafted clause returns control to the indemnified party in defined circumstances. These are the ones worth insisting on.

**Conflict of interest.** Where the parties' interests in the defense genuinely diverge, common counsel is untenable.

**Non-monetary relief.** Where the claim seeks an injunction, or anything that would constrain how the business operates, the party that has to live with the outcome should be running it.

**Criminal or regulatory proceedings.** Different stakes, different consequences, and an exposure that does not end with a payment.

**Claims exceeding the cap.** This one is the sharpest and the most frequently omitted. If the claim is worth more than the indemnifying party's remaining exposure under the cap, the economics invert. They are now controlling a litigation whose downside above the cap falls entirely on someone else — and their incentive to fight it hard disappears at precisely the point the other party's exposure begins.

## Where an insurer is involved, control is a three-way question

The contract allocates control between two parties. The policy may allocate it to a third.

Many liability policies give the insurer the right to appoint counsel, frequently from a **panel** of firms with pre-agreed rates. Where the insurer is funding the defense, that right can in practice override what the parties negotiated between themselves. The agreement says the indemnifying party controls and selects counsel reasonably satisfactory to the other side; the policy says the insurer appoints from its panel. The policy is paying.

This is not hypothetical. It surfaces in the first weeks of a covered claim, and it surprises people who negotiated the contract carefully and never read the policy.

## Defending under a reservation of rights

A further wrinkle, and an uncomfortable one.

An insurer will often fund a defense while **reserving its rights** — preserving the ability to deny coverage later, once the facts develop. The defense proceeds. The bills are paid. And the insurer retains the option to conclude that the matter was never covered.

This puts appointed counsel in a structurally awkward position. They are defending the insured, but were selected by, and are reporting to, a party that may ultimately be adverse to the insured on coverage. Facts developed in the defense can inform the coverage decision.

Where the conflict is material, some jurisdictions give the insured a right to **independent counsel** at the insurer's expense. Whether that right exists, and what triggers it, is jurisdiction-specific — consult qualified counsel in the relevant jurisdiction. What is not jurisdiction-specific is the need to notice the problem early rather than discovering it in month nine.

cards.back: The indemnifying party's defined window after notice — commonly 15-30 days — to take control of defending a third-party claim. Silence usually counts as declining.
Law firms an insurer appoints from at pre-agreed rates. Where the insurer funds the defense, this right can override the counsel-selection terms the parties negotiated.
An insurer funding a defense while preserving its ability to deny coverage later. Creates a structural conflict for insurer-appointed counsel.

questions.stem: Why should control of defense shift to the indemnified party when a claim exceeds the cap?
options: Because the indemnifying party's insurance will not respond above the cap
Because the indemnifying party would be controlling a litigation whose exposure above the cap falls entirely on the other party, removing their incentive to defend it hard
Because caps are unenforceable once a claim exceeds them
Because the indemnified party is better placed to negotiate a settlement
questions.explanation: Above the cap, the indemnifying party has no remaining financial stake. They are running a defense where every additional unit of liability lands on someone else — exactly the misalignment the carve-out exists to prevent.

lessons.title: Consent to settle: where interests genuinely diverge

blocks.markdown:
At some point in most live claims, one party wants to settle and the other does not.

It is tempting to read this as a failure of goodwill, or as one side being unreasonable. It is neither. The parties have different exposure, and different exposure produces different optimal settlements. The disagreement is structural, and a well-drafted consent provision assumes it will happen rather than hoping it won't.

## Why the optimal settlement differs

The indemnifying party is paying. Their interest is to resolve cheaply and early — a settlement at five is a good outcome on a claim that might cost twenty at trial.

But push the numbers and the logic inverts. If the claim is approaching the cap, the indemnifying party wants to settle at any figure below it and walk away. Everything above the cap lands on the other party, and a settlement that exhausts the cap is, from the payer's perspective, a complete resolution.

Meanwhile the indemnified party may want to settle for reasons that have nothing to do with the legal merits. The product is still on the market. The regulator is still watching. A defensible claim can still be worth settling to make it stop. To the indemnifying party, that looks like being asked to fund someone else's commercial convenience.

## And sometimes the cheap settlement is the expensive one

A settlement that includes an admission of liability, or a public filing conceding a point about product safety, may be financially attractive and commercially disastrous.

The payer sees a number. The operator sees a document that will be cited in every subsequent claim, quoted to a regulator, and produced in discovery in the next matter. These are not the same instrument.

## How the clause handles it

Two consent rights, running in opposite directions.

The indemnifying party, where it controls the defense, typically **cannot settle without the indemnified party's consent** where the settlement involves non-monetary relief, includes an admission of liability or wrongdoing, fails to include a full and unconditional release of the indemnified party, or exceeds the cap.

The indemnified party typically **cannot settle without the indemnifying party's consent** at all — and settling unilaterally usually forfeits the indemnity for that claim entirely. This is the harsher of the two, and it is standard.

Both are usually qualified by consent "not to be unreasonably withheld." What counts as unreasonable in this context is genuinely contested, and the phrase resolves less than it appears to.

## Symmetric in form, asymmetric in effect

The two consent rights look balanced on the page. They are not balanced in practice.

The party controlling the defense holds the initiative. It negotiates with the claimant, shapes the offer, and presents it. The other party is reacting to a proposal it did not build, under time pressure, with the threat of an unreasonable-withholding argument if it says no.

Which produces an uncomfortable general rule: the party with the most to lose from a trial often has the least leverage in the settlement negotiation, because the others can force its hand.

## With an insurer, three parties must align

The policy carries its own consent requirement, and it is usually the strictest of the three. An insured who settles without the insurer's consent can lose coverage for the settlement it just agreed to.

So the practical position on a covered claim is that no settlement happens unless the indemnifying party, the indemnified party, and the insurer all agree. Three-way unanimity, under deadline, between parties with different exposure.

## The hammer clause

This is the mechanism that breaks the deadlock, and it is worth knowing before you need it.

An insurer recommends settling at a given figure. The insured refuses and wants to fight on. A **hammer clause** — also called a settlement cap or, less politely, a blackmail clause — provides that the insurer's liability is then capped at that recommended figure plus defense costs incurred to that date. Everything beyond falls on the insured.

The insured is free to continue the fight. It is simply doing so on its own money from that point forward.

A **soft hammer** softens this by sharing the excess on an agreed split rather than shifting all of it — the insurer might bear seventy per cent of amounts above the recommended settlement. Whether a policy has a hard hammer, a soft hammer, or neither is a coverage term worth knowing at placement rather than discovering mid-claim.

cards.back: The standard qualifier on both parties' settlement consent rights. Resolves less than it appears to — what counts as unreasonable here is genuinely contested.
Caps the insurer's liability at a settlement figure it recommended and the insured refused, plus defense costs to that date. The insured may fight on, at its own expense.
A hammer clause sharing amounts above the recommended settlement on an agreed split — e.g. 70/30 — rather than shifting all of the excess to the insured.

questions.stem: Why does an indemnifying party's settlement incentive change as a claim approaches the cap?
options: Because caps are typically renegotiated once a claim approaches them
Because a settlement that exhausts the cap fully resolves their exposure, while everything above it falls on the other party
Because insurers require settlement once the cap is within reach
Because the duty to mitigate requires settlement at that point
questions.explanation: Below the cap the indemnifying party is spending its own money and wants a cheap resolution. At the cap, a settlement that uses it up ends their exposure entirely — and the risk of a worse outcome at trial belongs to someone else.

blocks.markdown:
Whoever controls the defense, the documents and the witnesses usually sit with the indemnified party. It is their business, their employees, their files.

That asymmetry is why cooperation provisions exist, and why they fall almost entirely on one side.

blocks.markdown:
## What cooperation actually requires

Produce documents. Make employees available for interviews and depositions. Give counsel access to records and systems. Provide the technical and regulatory knowledge the defense depends on.

In a pharma claim this is not a light obligation. A product liability matter can consume substantial time from regulatory affairs, pharmacovigilance, and medical affairs staff over a period of years.

Which raises a question agreements routinely fail to answer: **who pays for it?** Employee time, document review, third-party vendor costs for collection and hosting. If the cooperation clause is silent and the loss definition doesn't cover internal costs, the cooperating party absorbs them.

## Privilege is the part that goes wrong

Attorney-client privilege protects communications between a client and its counsel made for the purpose of legal advice. Disclosing privileged material to a third party generally waives that protection.

Cooperating on a defense means sharing exactly the kind of material privilege exists to protect: candid assessments of exposure, weaknesses in the position, internal views on what actually happened.

The doctrine that permits this without waiver is **common interest** — sometimes called joint defense privilege. Where two parties share a legal interest in a matter, communications between them in furtherance of that shared interest can retain protection.

## The limits of common interest

Three things to know, and the second is the one that catches people.

**It requires a shared legal interest, not merely a commercial one.** Both parties wanting the claim to go away is not enough. The interest must be identical or substantially similar in the legal position being advanced.

**It is fragile.** Common interest protects material shared while the interests align. If the parties later become adverse — a dispute about whether the indemnity applies at all, or a coverage fight — the protection may not survive into that second dispute. Candid analysis shared freely during the cooperative phase can surface in the argument about who bears the loss.

**Its scope varies by jurisdiction.** Some recognise it broadly, some narrowly, some barely at all. Consult qualified counsel in the relevant jurisdiction before assuming material is protected.

## Joint defense agreements

A **joint defense agreement** documents the common interest in writing: what is being shared, for what purpose, on what confidentiality terms, and what happens if the parties' interests later diverge.

It does not create privilege that would not otherwise exist. What it does is evidence the common interest, discipline what gets shared, and set the rules for the fallout in advance.

The divergence provisions are the ones worth reading. A well-drafted agreement addresses whether shared material can be used by one party against the other in a subsequent dispute between them. A badly drafted one leaves that to be argued later, at the worst possible moment.

## The policy cooperation duty runs in parallel

The policy imposes its own cooperation obligation, and it is enforced considerably harder than the contractual one.

Failure to cooperate with a counterparty is generally measured against prejudice — the same analysis that applies to late notice. Failure to cooperate with an insurer can **void coverage**. The consequence is categorical rather than proportionate.

## And the insurer creates its own privilege problem

An insurer needs the defense's candid assessment in order to reserve properly. Providing it means disclosing privileged analysis to a party that is not your counsel and may, on coverage, become your opponent.

Some jurisdictions treat insurer and insured as sharing a common interest for this purpose. Some do not, and disclosure to the insurer can waive privilege as against the claimant.

The position is worse where the insurer is defending under a reservation of rights, because it has already signalled potential adversity. You are handing your frank assessment of your own weaknesses to a party that has expressly reserved the right to deny you coverage on the basis of how the facts develop.

There is no universal answer here. There is only the discipline of asking the question before sending the memo rather than after.

The insurer's separate cooperation requirement. Breach can void coverage outright, where breach of a contractual cooperation duty is usually measured against prejudice.

lessons.title: Damages: direct, consequential, and the carve-outs that matter

blocks.markdown:
An indemnity is only worth what it lets you recover. Two clauses decide that: the definition of covered losses, and the damages exclusions.

Both tend to be read quickly because they look like definitions rather than deal terms. They are deal terms.

## The categories, and why the labels mislead

**Direct damages** flow naturally and immediately from the breach. If the seller warranted that equipment worked and it did not, the cost of repair is direct.

**Consequential damages** flow from the breach through the particular circumstances of the injured party. The profits lost while the equipment was down are consequential — they depend on facts about that business rather than on the breach alone. In common law systems these are generally recoverable only where they were foreseeable, or known to the breaching party, at the time of contracting.

**Incidental damages** are the costs of dealing with the breach itself: investigation, mitigation, sourcing a replacement.

**Punitive damages** are rarely available in contract at all, and are commonly excluded expressly for the avoidance of doubt.

Here is the problem with those labels.

Contracts routinely exclude "consequential, indirect and special damages" as though the three were a single concept with a settled meaning. They are not. Courts do not treat them identically, "special damages" carries a distinct technical meaning in some jurisdictions, and civil law systems frame the whole question differently — often through foreseeability and causation rather than a taxonomy of damage types.

Stacking the words is not the same as defining them. An exclusion built from a list of labels rather than a description of what is excluded is an invitation to argue.

## The lost profits fight

Every negotiation reaches this, and there is no clean answer.

Are lost profits direct or consequential? It depends on the facts. Where the entire commercial purpose of the contract was to generate those profits, a strong argument exists that they are direct. Where they depend on the injured party's particular downstream arrangements, they look consequential.

Which is why the drafting matters more than the category. An exclusion of "consequential damages" leaves the argument open. An exclusion of "consequential damages, **including lost profits**" closes it. Those two clauses look similar on the page and produce materially different outcomes.

Read every damages exclusion for whether lost profits are named. If they are not, somebody is going to argue about it.

## Why a consequential damages exclusion can gut an M&A indemnity

In a commercial supply agreement, excluding consequential damages is unremarkable. In an acquisition it can hollow out the indemnity entirely.

Consider a seller who overstated the target's EBITDA by one million. What is the buyer's loss?

If the answer is one million, the indemnity has limited value. But the buyer did not pay one times EBITDA. It paid a multiple — say eight. The overstatement caused it to overpay by eight million, not one.

This is the **multiple-based damages** question, and it is one of the most consequential fights in any acquisition indemnity. Buyers argue the loss is the overpayment, measured on the multiple they actually paid. Sellers argue the loss is the shortfall itself, and frequently insist on express language excluding damages calculated on a multiple, valuation or similar basis.

Whoever wins that drafting point has moved the value of the indemnity by a factor of eight.

## Liquidated damages

A **liquidated damages** provision fixes a sum payable on a specified breach, substituting for proof of actual loss.

The attraction is certainty. Where a loss is real but genuinely hard to quantify — delay in a technology transfer, failure to hit a regulatory milestone, breach of an exclusivity undertaking — a pre-agreed figure removes the need to prove a number that may be unprovable.

The risk is enforceability. Common law systems distinguish liquidated damages, which are enforceable, from **penalties**, which are not. The historical test asked whether the sum was a genuine pre-estimate of loss or was punitive in purpose. Modern English authority reframed it around whether the sum is out of all proportion to any legitimate interest the innocent party had in enforcement.

Civil law systems generally take a different route: rather than voiding an excessive stipulated sum, courts often have power to reduce it. Same commercial concern, different mechanism, materially different outcome if you are the party relying on the clause.

This is jurisdiction-sensitive enough that the governing law choice — lesson 15 — directly determines whether a liquidated damages clause is an asset or decoration.

## Mitigation, and the deductions that shrink a recovery

The loss you claim is not the loss you recover.

A **duty to mitigate** applies — you cannot let a loss run and present the bill. Failure to take reasonable steps reduces recovery by whatever those steps would have avoided.

Beyond that, most well-drafted loss definitions are expressed **net of** several things:

- **Insurance proceeds** actually received in respect of the loss
- **Third-party recoveries** from other sources
- **Tax benefits** realised as a result of the loss

Each of these is reasonable in principle and contestable in application. Net of insurance proceeds *received*, or proceeds *recoverable* whether or not pursued? The second obliges you to claim on your own policy before calling on the indemnity, with consequences for your premiums and your future coverage that the indemnifying party does not bear.

lessons.title: Caps, baskets, and de minimis: the financial architecture

blocks.markdown:
Three provisions filter what an indemnity actually pays: a floor on individual claims, a floor on aggregate claims, and a ceiling on total recovery.

Each is straightforward alone. The value sits in how they interact, and in one word buried in the basket definition that can change a recovery by a factor of six.

blocks.caption: Small claims are discarded before they count. The aggregate must cross a threshold before anything is payable, and a ceiling limits the total.
blocks.alt: A cross-section of an upright cylindrical vessel containing stacked blocks of varying thickness, filling it to about half its height. A lower etched reference line crosses through the stack; an upper line sits near the rim with a wide empty gap above the blocks. Several much smaller blocks lie discarded on the surface outside the vessel, and one greyed-out block rests above the rim, excluded.

blocks.markdown:
## The de minimis threshold

A floor on individual claims. Anything below it is disregarded entirely.

The logic is administrative rather than economic. Neither party benefits from a process that entertains claims costing more to assess than they are worth.

The trap is aggregation. Many small breaches arising from the same underlying problem — a systematic error in how a compliance process was run, say — can each fall below the threshold while amounting to something substantial together. Whether they can be grouped depends on whether the agreement contains an aggregation provision allowing claims arising from the same facts or the same breach to be treated as one.

Without it, a pattern of small failures is unrecoverable no matter how large the pattern.

## The basket, and the word that matters

A floor on aggregate claims. Until total losses exceed it, nothing is payable.

The rationale is sound: representations about a real operating business can never be perfect, and a seller should not face liability for ordinary variance. The basket absorbs it.

But there are two kinds, and they behave completely differently once crossed.

values: Recovery only of the excess above the threshold
Once the threshold is exceeded, recover from the first unit

Basket of 1m, losses of 1.2m, recover 1.2m

attributes.label: Role of the threshold

blocks.markdown:
Note what happens near the threshold. With a basket of one million and losses of 1.01 million, a deductible basket pays ten thousand and a tipping basket pays 1.01 million.

The clause is a single sentence and the two versions look almost identical. One word — whether recovery is of losses "in excess of" the threshold or of "all losses" once the threshold is exceeded — carries the whole difference.

## The cap

A ceiling on aggregate recovery, and rarely a single number.

Most regimes tier it. A **general cap** covers ordinary business representations — commonly a modest percentage of deal value. **Fundamental representations** (title to the assets or shares, due authority, capitalisation) carry a substantially higher cap or none at all, because a failure there goes to whether the buyer got what it paid for. **Tax** is frequently separate again, and **fraud** is essentially always uncapped.

The practical consequence is that "the cap" is usually the wrong question. The right question is which cap applies to the claim you actually have.

## How the three interact

A claim has to clear every layer in sequence.

First it must exceed the de minimis threshold on its own, or it is disregarded — and typically does not even count toward the basket. Then it joins the aggregate. Once the aggregate exceeds the basket, recovery begins — of the excess only, or of everything, depending on the basket type. And the total is then limited by whichever cap applies.

Work it through with real numbers. Deal value of 100. De minimis of 0.05. Basket of 1. General cap of 10.

Four claims arrive: 0.03, 0.2, 0.4 and 0.6.

The first is disregarded — below de minimis, and it does not count toward the basket either. The remaining three aggregate to 1.2, which clears the basket. With a deductible basket the recovery is 0.2. With a tipping basket it is 1.2.

Same four claims. Same cap. Six times the recovery.

## What this means in negotiation

The cap gets the attention because it is the largest number. It is frequently the least important of the three.

Most indemnity claims in practice are far smaller than the cap. They are decided by the de minimis threshold, by whether aggregation is permitted, and above all by the basket type. A buyer that concedes a deductible basket to win two percentage points on the cap has almost certainly made a bad trade.

Recovery only of losses above the aggregate threshold. Basket of 1m and losses of 1.2m yields 0.2m. The threshold stays with the buyer permanently.
Once aggregate losses exceed the threshold, recovery runs from the first unit. Basket of 1m and losses of 1.2m yields 1.2m. Also called a first-dollar basket.
Title, due authority, capitalisation — reps going to whether the buyer received what it paid for. Carry a much higher cap or none, and usually a longer survival period.

lessons.title: Survival periods: when your protection expires

blocks.markdown:
Representations do not last forever. Each one survives closing for a defined period, and when that period ends the indemnity resting on it ends with it.

After expiry, a breach that has existed since before closing and that nobody discovered is simply the buyer's problem. Permanently.

## Why twelve to twenty-four months

General business representations commonly survive for somewhere between one and two years, and the number is not arbitrary.

The logic is the audit cycle. A buyer that has been through one full annual audit of the acquired business has had a genuine opportunity to surface accounting, compliance and operational problems. Survival periods in that range give the buyer that cycle and then close the book.

Which also tells you what the period is not designed to catch: anything that takes longer than one operating year to become visible.

## The tiering

Different representations get different periods, on a consistent logic — the harder a problem is to discover, or the more fundamental it is, the longer the tail.

**Fundamental representations** — title, authority, capitalisation — survive far longer, often to the statutory limitation period or indefinitely. A defect in title does not become the buyer's problem because eighteen months elapsed.

**Tax representations** are usually tied to the relevant statutory assessment period, because that is how long the authority has to raise the issue.

**Intellectual property** often sits at an intermediate period, on the view that infringement claims surface slowly.

**Specific indemnities** for identified risks run on their own clocks, frequently until the identified matter is finally resolved.

**Covenants** survive until performed, or for a stated period afterward.

## Notified, or resolved?

This distinction decides whether a survival period is workable or a trap.

The standard and sensible position is that a claim **notified** before expiry survives until it is finally resolved, however long that takes. The survival period governs when you must raise the claim, not when you must finish it.

Some provisions say something harsher. A requirement that the claim be **resolved**, or that formal proceedings be **commenced**, within the survival period is a materially different obligation — and on a third-party claim that will run for years, potentially an impossible one.

Read for which it is. A twenty-four month survival requiring resolution within the period is not a twenty-four month survival.

## The notice problem, again

Lesson 4 covered the notice trap in direct claims. Survival is where it bites hardest.

A buyer discovers something in month twenty. The breach is real. The survival period ends at month twenty-four. But the notice provision requires a good-faith estimate of the loss, and the investigation will not conclude for another year.

The buyer either serves a notice that can be attacked as deficient, or serves nothing and loses the claim at month twenty-four. Both are bad, and the choice was determined at signing by whether anyone negotiated for "to the extent then determinable."

## The pharma latency problem

Here the standard architecture fits the industry badly.

Product liability and regulatory exposure in pharma surface on timescales that have nothing to do with audit cycles. A safety signal can emerge in year four. A regulatory inspection finding can arise from conduct years earlier. A patent challenge can be filed long after any general representation has expired.

A twenty-four month survival period does not address any of that. Which is why deals in this sector handle the long tail through other mechanisms:

- **Specific indemnities** with extended or open-ended periods for known product and regulatory issues
- **Product liability insurance**, which operates on policy terms rather than contractual survival
- **Reps and warranties insurance**, whose policy period can extend well beyond the contractual survival and is one of the main reasons buyers pursue it

If the exposure that actually worries you is a latent product issue, the survival period is the wrong instrument to be negotiating. Lesson 13 covers the ones that are.

cards.back: How long a representation and the indemnity for its breach remain live after closing. Once expired, an undiscovered pre-closing breach becomes permanently the buyer's.
Standard drafting lets a claim notified before expiry survive until finally resolved. A provision requiring resolution or commencement of proceedings within the period is far harsher.
It gives the buyer one full post-closing audit cycle to surface problems. It is not designed to catch anything that takes longer than an operating year to become visible.

Because product liability, regulatory and IP exposure surface on timescales unrelated to an audit cycle, often years after closing
Because regulatory approvals cannot be transferred within 24 months
Because insurers require survival periods to exceed 36 months
questions.explanation: The 12-24 month convention is built around giving a buyer one audit cycle. Latent safety signals, inspection findings and patent challenges do not respect that timetable, which is why the long tail is handled through specific indemnities and insurance rather than through survival.

lessons.title: Escrow and holdback: securing the recovery

blocks.markdown:
An indemnity is a promise to pay. Its value depends entirely on the promisor still existing, and still being solvent, when the claim arrives.

That is not a given. A private equity seller will distribute proceeds to its investors and wind up the holding vehicle. A corporate seller disposing of an asset may dissolve the entity that gave the representations. Three years later there may be nothing to sue.

An uncapped indemnity from a party that no longer exists is worth less than a small escrow from one that does.

blocks.caption: Funds held where neither party can reach them alone.
blocks.alt: A sturdy banded metal strongbox drawn in isometric technical style, closed, with two separate brass keyholes side by side on its front face. Two keys lie far apart from one another in front of the box, neither inserted.

blocks.markdown:
## Escrow

A portion of the purchase price is placed with a third-party escrow agent at closing, held under an agreement specifying when it releases and what happens if a claim is pending.

The mechanics worth negotiating:

**Amount.** Often a percentage of deal value, sometimes matching the general cap, sometimes a fraction of it.

**Release schedule.** A single release at expiry of the general survival period, or tranches releasing progressively. Tranches favour the seller by returning capital sooner.

**Pending claims at a release date.** A properly drafted escrow retains the amount of any notified but unresolved claim past the scheduled release and returns the balance.

**Interest.** The escrowed funds earn something. Who receives it is negotiable and frequently overlooked.

**Agent fees.** Modest, but someone pays them.

## Holdback

The cheaper alternative: the buyer simply retains part of the price rather than depositing it with an agent.

No escrow agent, no fees, less documentation. And a materially worse position for the seller, because the buyer is now holding the money.

The seller bears the buyer's credit risk. The seller has to ask for release rather than having a neutral party administer it. And the buyer has an obvious incentive, at each release date, to find a reason the funds should stay where they are.

Holdbacks are common in smaller transactions and where the parties have a relationship that makes the arrangement comfortable. They are a poor structure where the counterparty is unfamiliar or the amount is significant.

blocks.markdown:
## The question that matters most

Is the escrow the **exclusive** source of recovery, or merely security for it?

If exclusive, the escrow is the real cap regardless of what the cap clause says. A ten per cent cap backed by a five per cent exclusive escrow is a five per cent cap with extra steps.

If the escrow is security only, the buyer can exhaust it and continue against the seller up to the contractual cap — assuming the seller is still there, which returns us to where this lesson started.

This single point often moves the economics of an indemnity package more than the cap negotiation does, and it sits in the escrow agreement rather than the purchase agreement, where it receives less attention.

## Separate escrows for known risks

Where a specific indemnity covers an identified matter — litigation already on foot, a regulatory issue under discussion — it is common to escrow separately against it, released when that matter resolves rather than on the general schedule.

This keeps a known, sizeable exposure from consuming the general escrow that exists to cover unknown problems. It also avoids the seller's capital being tied up on the general timetable for a risk that may resolve much sooner, or much later.

## What insurance changes

Where reps and warranties insurance is in place, the escrow often shrinks dramatically or disappears.

The security function has been transferred. The buyer's recourse is to an insurer with a balance sheet rather than to a seller who may be gone, and the seller keeps its proceeds at closing instead of leaving them on deposit for two years.

That trade is one of the main commercial drivers behind the growth of R&W insurance, and it is the subject of the next lesson.

The buyer retains part of the price rather than escrowing it. Cheaper and simpler, but the seller bears the buyer's credit risk and must ask for release.

lessons.title: Insurance and R&W insurance: shifting the risk

blocks.markdown:
The insurer has appeared in every procedural lesson so far. A second notice clock in the first thirty days. A third party with a right to appoint counsel. A consent requirement that has to align with two others. A cooperation duty enforced harder than the contractual one.

This lesson stops treating it as an intrusion into the two-party model and looks at it directly.

blocks.caption: An insurance programme is built in layers: a retention the insured bears, a primary policy above it, and excess layers attaching above that.
blocks.alt: Four solid horizontal slabs stacked in a single aligned column, drawn in isometric technical cross-section. The bottom slab is much the thinnest and darkest; each slab above is thicker, with the palest and thickest at the top. Crisp boundaries separate the four layers.

blocks.markdown:
## The distinction that decides pharma coverage

Two policy structures, and the difference is not a technicality.

An **occurrence-based** policy covers events that occurred during the policy period, whenever the claim arrives. A product sold in 2019 under an occurrence policy in force that year is covered when a claim lands in 2026.

A **claims-made** policy covers claims made during the policy period, whenever the event occurred. The same product, insured under a claims-made policy that lapsed at closing, is not covered when that claim arrives — because the claim was not made while the policy was live.

For an industry whose exposure surfaces years after the product was sold, this is the single most consequential coverage term. It is also the one most likely to be treated as a procurement detail rather than a deal issue.

Two mechanisms soften a claims-made structure, and both need to be in place before you need them.

A **retroactive date** sets how far back the policy will reach for events. A claims-made policy with a retroactive date after the products in question were sold covers nothing relevant.

**Tail coverage** — also called run-off or an extended reporting period — buys the right to report claims for a defined period after the policy ends. On a transaction where the selling entity will cease to exist, tail coverage is often the only thing standing between a long-tail claim and nobody at all.

## Layers, and who runs the early defense

A programme is usually built in layers: a primary policy, then excess layers attaching above it.

Beneath the primary sits either a deductible or a self-insured retention, and the difference affects control rather than just money.

With a **deductible**, the insurer typically administers the claim from the outset and recoups the deductible from the insured. With a **self-insured retention**, the insured pays and manages the matter until the retention is exhausted, and the insurer's duties — including its right to appoint counsel — do not engage until then.

So on a claim that will resolve inside the retention, the insured is running its own defense with its own counsel. On a claim that will pierce it, control changes hands partway through, usually at an awkward moment.

## The gap between two insurance programmes

At closing, the seller's policies and the buyer's policies both exist, and neither was written with this transaction in mind.

Who insures a product manufactured and sold before closing, for a claim arriving after it? The seller's occurrence policies may well respond — but the seller has no commercial incentive to pursue coverage for the buyer's benefit, and in an asset deal the entity holding those policies may be winding up.

The mechanisms are assignment of insurance rights, or having the buyer named as an additional insured under the relevant historic policies. Both need to be negotiated at signing and both are routinely forgotten, leaving a period of exposure that no policy covers and no party expected.

## Subrogation reopens closed relationships

When an insurer pays, it generally acquires the insured's rights against whoever caused the loss and can pursue them directly. That is **subrogation**.

The practical consequence is uncomfortable. An insurer that has paid a claim can proceed against your counterparty — a supplier, a distribution partner, the other side of the very deal you just closed — on your behalf and without much regard for the commercial relationship you were hoping to preserve.

Which is why waiver of subrogation provisions exist, and why they are worth looking for in any agreement with a party you intend to keep working with.

## Reps and warranties insurance

A distinct product, and one that has reshaped how indemnity packages are negotiated.

A **buy-side R&W policy** — much the more common form — lets the buyer claim directly against an insurer for breach of the seller's representations, rather than against the seller. The seller's exposure shrinks or disappears.

What it changes at the negotiating table is substantial: smaller caps, shorter survival periods, minimal or no escrow, and a seller that walks away at closing with its proceeds rather than leaving them on deposit for two years. For a private equity seller that needs to distribute and wind up, that clean exit is often the point of the whole exercise.

## What R&W insurance does not cover

The exclusions matter more than the coverage, and several are structural rather than negotiable.

**Known issues.** Anything surfaced in diligence or disclosed in the schedules is excluded. The policy insures unknown breaches. A known problem still needs a specific indemnity from the seller.

**Purchase price adjustments** and forward-looking statements — projections, forecasts, budgets.

**And, frequently in this sector, sector-specific carve-outs.** Product liability, regulatory compliance and certain intellectual property matters are commonly excluded or heavily sub-limited in pharma policies, precisely because they are the exposures underwriters least want. The result is that R&W insurance may cover the representations you were least worried about and exclude the ones you were.

Read the exclusions before treating the policy as a substitute for a seller indemnity.

blocks.markdown:
## One dynamic worth noticing

R&W insurance tends to de-escalate the indemnity negotiation, because neither party is arguing quite so hard about its own money.

But the scrutiny does not disappear — it moves. Underwriters read the diligence reports, ask about gaps, and price or exclude accordingly. A thin diligence process that might have survived a negotiation with a motivated seller will not survive underwriting.

The discipline is still applied. It is simply applied by someone else, later, and with the power to exclude rather than to argue.

cards.back: Occurrence covers events during the policy period whenever claimed. Claims-made covers claims made during the period whenever the event occurred. For long-tail pharma exposure this decides everything.
Also run-off or extended reporting period. Buys the right to report claims after a claims-made policy ends. Often the only recourse where the insured entity will cease to exist.

With an SIR the insured pays and manages the claim until exhaustion, and the insurer's duties do not engage until then. With a deductible the insurer usually administers from the start and recoups it.
An insurer that pays acquires the insured's rights against whoever caused the loss, and can pursue them — including a counterparty you intended to keep working with.

questions.stem: Why is the occurrence versus claims-made distinction especially decisive in pharma?
options: Because regulators require occurrence-based cover for marketed products
Because exposure surfaces years after sale, so a lapsed claims-made policy leaves the pre-closing period uncovered while an occurrence policy still responds
Because claims-made policies cannot be written for pharmaceutical products
Because occurrence policies carry no retention
questions.explanation: An occurrence policy responds based on when the event happened, so a policy in force when the product was sold covers a claim arriving years later. A claims-made policy that lapsed at closing does not, because the claim was never made while it was live.

lessons.title: Pharma-specific claims: product liability, IP, regulatory

blocks.markdown:
Three claim types dominate pharma indemnity exposure, and they behave so differently that a package calibrated for one will handle the others badly.

They differ in when they surface, who the claimant is, whether the exposure is monetary, and — in one case — whether the indemnity's machinery even fits.

## Product liability

The long tail. A claim can arise years after the product was sold, brought by someone with no relationship to either party to the transaction.

Three features shape how it interacts with an indemnity.

**Latency**, which lesson 11 covered: the exposure outlives ordinary survival periods, so it is handled through specific indemnities and insurance rather than general representations.

**Multiplicity.** One defect produces many claimants. The aggregate can dwarf any cap, and a de minimis threshold designed to screen trivial claims does nothing useful against a hundred individually modest ones — which is where the aggregation provision from lesson 10 earns its place.

**Pharmacovigilance.** Adverse event reporting obligations transfer with the product. A pre-closing failure to report creates exposure on two fronts at once: product liability to the claimant, and regulatory exposure for the reporting failure itself.

## The point that catches dealmakers

In an asset deal, the parties allocate pre-closing product liability to the seller. The buyer is indemnified. Everyone is satisfied.

Then a claimant sues the buyer.

The indemnity allocates risk **between the parties to it**. It does not determine who a third party may sue. And in a number of jurisdictions, **successor liability** doctrines allow a claimant to pursue the acquirer of a product line for injuries caused by units the seller manufactured — on continuation-of-product-line or similar reasoning — regardless of how the purchase agreement allocated it.

The contractual allocation still works. It simply works as a right of recovery *after* the buyer has been sued, defended, and paid. Which makes the seller's survival, solvency and security — lesson 12 — the thing that determines whether the allocation was real.

Whether successor liability applies, and on what basis, is jurisdiction-specific. Consult qualified counsel in the relevant jurisdiction.

## Intellectual property infringement

A third party asserts that the product infringes its rights. In generics this is close to an operating condition rather than a contingency.

What makes IP claims procedurally distinct is the remedy. A product liability claimant wants money. An IP claimant frequently wants the product **off the market** — and an injunction is not something an indemnity can make good.

This is why the non-monetary relief carve-out from lesson 6 matters here specifically. A seller controlling the defense of an infringement claim is optimising to limit a payment. The buyer is trying to keep a product on sale. Those are not the same defense, and the party that has to live with the outcome should be running it.

Two distinctions worth holding separately: a claim that **you infringe someone else's** right, and a challenge seeking to **invalidate a right you acquired**. The first threatens your ability to sell. The second threatens the value of what you bought. Different exposures, different reps, and frequently different indemnities.

## Regulatory and compliance

Here the indemnity machinery fits worst, and the reason is structural.

The third-party claim procedure from lessons 5 through 8 assumes an adversarial proceeding: a claimant, a defense, counsel, a settlement. A regulatory exposure often has none of those. An inspection finding, a warning letter, a suspension of a marketing authorisation, a mandated recall — a regulator does not sue you, it acts.

So ask whether the agreement's definition of "third-party claim" actually captures a regulatory action. Frequently it is drafted around litigation and captures regulatory proceedings only awkwardly or not at all. Then ask who controls the response to a regulator, because "control of the defense" is close to meaningless when the counterparty is an authority you must maintain a relationship with indefinitely.

## Two regulatory exposures worth naming

**Anti-bribery and corruption.** Pre-closing conduct in higher-risk markets creates post-closing exposure for the acquirer, and it interacts badly with the rest of the package. Discovery of an issue may trigger a disclosure obligation to authorities — which is the opposite of a defense strategy, and a decision the buyer may be required to take over the seller's objection even though the seller bears the indemnity.

**Data protection.** Clinical, pharmacovigilance and patient data carry exposure under regimes with meaningful penalties and their own notification timetables, again measured in hours and days rather than the weeks a contractual notice provision contemplates.

In both cases the regulatory clock runs faster than the indemnity clock, and the obligations are owed to someone who is not a party to your agreement.

cards.back: Doctrines allowing a claimant to pursue the acquirer of a product line for injuries from units the seller made, regardless of contractual allocation. The indemnity becomes a right of recovery after being sued, not a shield.

A claim that you infringe another's right threatens your ability to sell. A challenge to invalidate a right you acquired threatens the value of what you bought. Different exposures and often different indemnities.

cards.front: Why regulatory exposure fits the machinery badly
cards.back: The third-party claim procedure assumes a claimant, a defense and a settlement. A regulator does not sue — it inspects, warns, suspends or mandates a recall. Check whether the definition of claim even captures it.

questions.stem: What does successor liability mean for a buyer that has been indemnified against pre-closing product liability?
options: The indemnity is unenforceable to the extent successor liability applies
The claimant may still sue the buyer directly, so the indemnity operates as a right of recovery after the buyer has defended and paid
The seller becomes the sole permissible defendant once the indemnity is in place
Successor liability only applies where the buyer acquires shares rather than assets
questions.explanation: The indemnity allocates risk between the parties to it and cannot bind a third party's choice of defendant. The buyer may be sued, defend, pay, and then recover — which makes the seller's continued existence and the security behind the indemnity decisive.

lessons.title: Choice of law: which law governs, and why it changes outcomes

blocks.markdown:
The governing law clause sits at the back of the agreement, runs to one sentence, and is frequently agreed in the last hour of a negotiation as a concession worth giving.

It determines how everything in front of it will be read.

## What the governing law actually decides

For an indemnity package specifically:

**How damages are characterised.** Whether lost profits are direct or consequential, and what an exclusion of consequential damages actually excludes — the fight from lesson 9 — is resolved by the governing law, not by the clause alone.

**Whether liquidated damages survive.** A common law court may strike a stipulated sum as a penalty. A civil law court is more likely to reduce it. The same clause is an asset under one law and decoration under another.

**Whether a general duty of good faith applies.** Civil law systems typically impose one. English law generally does not, outside specific relationships. This matters directly to how a party may exercise a discretion — withholding consent to a settlement, for instance, where lesson 7 left the meaning of "unreasonably" unresolved.

**How ambiguity is resolved.** Whether ambiguity is construed against the drafter, how much weight is given to the words alone versus the parties' intent, and whether pre-contractual negotiations can be looked at at all — English law is markedly more textual than most civil law systems.
