blocks.markdown:
## Why particular laws get chosen

**English law** is chosen for predictability. A deep body of commercial jurisprudence, strong respect for freedom of contract, effective entire agreement clauses, and no general good faith duty to introduce uncertainty into how discretions are exercised. It favours the party that wants the words to mean what they say.

**New York law** offers comparable depth with a well-developed M&A case law, and is the default where a US counterparty is involved.

**Swiss law** is chosen for neutrality, particularly where neither party wants the other's home law and where an arbitration is seated in Switzerland. It is a civil law system: a general good faith duty applies, and courts have power to reduce excessive contractual penalties rather than striking them.

None of these is better. They allocate interpretive risk differently, and which allocation suits you depends on which side of the agreement you are on and which clauses you are relying on.

## The limits of the choice

A governing law clause does not displace everything.

**Mandatory rules** apply regardless. Product liability regimes imposing strict liability on producers cannot be contracted away as against an injured claimant. Regulatory obligations attach to the holder of the authorisation under the law of the territory. Competition law applies where the effects are felt. Local mandatory provisions may govern aspects of performance wherever it occurs.

**Limitation periods** deserve separate attention. Some jurisdictions restrict how far parties may contract out of statutory limitation — which can undercut a negotiated survival period from either direction, making a long one unenforceable or a short one ineffective.

## The distinction that closes the lesson

The governing law governs your agreement with your counterparty. It does not govern a third party's claim against you.

A patient injured in Germany sues under German law. A regulator in Saudi Arabia acts under its own authority. A competitor asserting a patent in France litigates under French law. None of them is a party to your purchase agreement and none is affected by the law you chose to govern it.

So a cross-border pharma deal runs two distinct legal questions in parallel. Your indemnity operates under one law. The claims it is meant to protect against arise under others, in territories you may never have negotiated about.

That is also why the forum you chose for disputes with your counterparty — the next lesson — is a separate decision from the law governing the contract, and why people who treat the two as one clause tend to get both wrong.

cards.back: Governing law is which substantive law interprets the contract. Jurisdiction or forum is where disputes are heard. Two separate decisions, frequently drafted as though they were one.

Civil law systems generally impose a duty of good faith in performance; English law generally does not in ordinary commercial contracts. Affects how discretions — like withholding settlement consent — may be exercised.

Rules applying regardless of the parties' choice of law: strict product liability toward claimants, regulatory obligations in the territory, competition law, and limits on contracting out of limitation periods.

questions.stem: Why does choosing English law not protect against a product liability claim brought by a patient in Germany?
options: Because English law expressly defers to EU product liability rules
Because the governing law binds only the parties to the agreement, while the claimant sues under the law of their own jurisdiction
Because product liability claims are always heard in the claimant's home courts under the contract's governing law
Because governing law clauses do not survive closing
questions.explanation: The governing law clause allocates interpretive risk between the contracting parties. A third-party claimant is not a party to that agreement and brings their claim under the applicable law of their own jurisdiction, frequently under a strict liability regime that cannot be contracted away.

lessons.title: Courts or arbitration: designing the dispute clause

blocks.markdown:
Governing law decides how the agreement is read. The forum decides who reads it, under what procedure, and whether the outcome can be appealed.

They are separate decisions. Drafting them as a single clause — which is common — is how parties end up with a law they chose deliberately and a forum they chose by accident.

## The real tradeoff

Arbitration is usually presented as faster and cheaper than litigation. For most commercial disputes of any size, that is not reliably true.

What arbitration genuinely offers is neutrality, confidentiality, a decision-maker the parties chose and who may actually understand the sector, procedural flexibility, and — the decisive one in cross-border deals — an award that travels. Lesson 17 covers that last point, and for many transactions it settles the question on its own.

What it costs you is the appeal. An arbitral award is final. An error of law is generally not reviewable anywhere. Finality is an advantage until the tribunal gets it wrong.

blocks.markdown:
## The seat is the term that matters most

And it is the term most often confused with something else.

The **seat** is the legal home of the arbitration. It determines the procedural law governing the arbitration itself, which courts have supervisory jurisdiction over it, and the nationality of the resulting award for enforcement purposes. Only the courts of the seat can set an award aside.

The **venue** is simply where the hearings physically happen. An arbitration seated in Switzerland can hold hearings in Dubai without becoming a Dubai arbitration.

That distinction has real consequences. Choosing a seat whose courts are interventionist, or whose judiciary is inexperienced with arbitration, imports a supervisory regime you did not intend. Choosing a seat in a state that is not party to the main enforcement framework undermines the principal reason you chose arbitration.

## The rest of the clause

**Institution or ad hoc.** An institutional arbitration — ICC, LCIA, SCC, the Swiss Rules, SIAC, HKIAC — is administered: the institution appoints where parties fail to, manages fees, and in some cases scrutinises the draft award before it issues. That administration costs money and is generally worth it. Ad hoc arbitration, typically under the UNCITRAL Rules, is cheaper and demands considerably more from the parties and the tribunal.

**One arbitrator or three.** Three costs roughly three times as much in tribunal fees and moves more slowly. For a mid-size dispute a sole arbitrator is usually the better answer, and a well-drafted clause can make this conditional — sole arbitrator below an agreed threshold, three above it.

**Language.** State it. Do not leave it to be argued.

**Scope.** "Any dispute arising out of or in connection with this agreement" is broad and deliberate. A narrower formulation invites a preliminary fight about whether the particular dispute falls inside the arbitration agreement at all.

**Interim relief.** Most institutional rules now provide an emergency arbitrator. That does not remove the need for court support, particularly for relief against third parties or anything requiring state enforcement power. Preserve the right to go to court for urgent measures without that being treated as a waiver of the arbitration agreement.

## Confidentiality is not automatic

Arbitration is commonly described as confidential. Whether it actually is depends on the rules chosen and the law of the seat, and the default is less protective than most people assume.

If confidentiality matters — and in pharma, where the dispute may concern safety data, pricing or a regulatory position, it usually does — it needs to be addressed expressly rather than assumed.

## Pathological clauses

A badly drafted dispute clause produces a dispute about the dispute, resolved before the substance is reached, at a cost of months and considerable fees.

The recurring failures: naming an institution that does not exist, or naming it wrongly; specifying one institution's rules and another's appointing authority; providing for arbitration and simultaneously conferring exclusive jurisdiction on a court; requiring an arbitrator with qualifications no available candidate holds; and multi-tier clauses drafted as mandatory conditions precedent, which hand the other side a jurisdictional objection that the negotiation or mediation stage was never properly exhausted.

Tiered escalation can be genuinely useful. Drafted as a hard precondition rather than an expectation, it becomes a weapon for the party that wants delay.

## What it actually takes

Be realistic at signing about what you are choosing.

An institutional arbitration of a mid-size commercial dispute commonly runs somewhere between one and two years from request to award, and considerably longer where the matter is technically complex or the tribunal is difficult to constitute. Total costs — tribunal, institution, counsel, experts — frequently reach a meaningful percentage of the amount in dispute, and the proportion rises sharply as the amount falls.

Which means arbitration is a poor forum for small disputes. A clause that sends every disagreement to a three-member ICC tribunal has made low-value claims uneconomic to pursue, which is a substantive outcome disguised as a procedural choice.

cards.back: The seat is the arbitration's legal home: it sets the procedural law, which courts supervise, and the award's nationality for enforcement. The venue is only where hearings physically occur.
Institutional arbitration is administered by a body that appoints, manages fees and may scrutinise awards. Ad hoc is cheaper and requires more of the parties and tribunal.

A dispute resolution clause defective enough to produce a fight about where to fight — non-existent institutions, inconsistent rules, arbitration plus exclusive court jurisdiction, or mandatory tiers used as a jurisdictional objection.

questions.stem: Why is the choice of seat more consequential than the choice of hearing venue?
options: Because hearings must be held in the seat unless both parties agree otherwise
Because the seat determines the arbitration's procedural law, which courts may supervise or set aside the award, and the award's nationality for enforcement
Because arbitrators must be qualified in the law of the seat
Because the seat determines the governing law of the contract
questions.explanation: The seat is the arbitration's legal home. It fixes the supervisory jurisdiction, the procedural law, and the award's nationality for enforcement purposes. The venue is a logistical matter — a Swiss-seated arbitration can hold hearings anywhere.

lessons.title: Enforcement across borders: where a win becomes money

blocks.markdown:
Winning is not recovering.

A judgment or award is a piece of paper establishing that you are owed something. Turning it into money requires a court in the place where the assets sit to give it effect. If that court will not, the paper is worth what the paper is worth.

This is the lesson that should change how you read a dispute resolution clause, because it is decided at signing and discovered years later.

## The asymmetry

**Arbitral awards travel.** A long-standing multilateral convention obliges contracting states — the large majority of commercially relevant jurisdictions — to recognise and enforce awards made in other contracting states, on limited and defined grounds of refusal. This framework is the single strongest practical argument for arbitration in cross-border transactions.

**Court judgments largely do not.** There is no equivalent global treaty for judgments. Within Europe, reciprocal frameworks provide near-automatic recognition between member states and certain neighbours including Switzerland. Outside those frameworks, enforcement of a foreign judgment depends on bilateral treaties where they exist, or on the enforcing state's own recognition rules, which range from workable to effectively closed.

So an English court judgment against a counterparty whose assets sit outside any applicable framework can be extremely difficult to enforce. An arbitral award against the same counterparty is materially easier. That difference, not speed or cost, is usually what should decide the forum in a deal with an emerging-market or Gulf counterparty.

Treaty membership and the state of newer instruments change over time. Check the current position for the specific jurisdictions in play rather than relying on a general rule — consult qualified counsel in the relevant jurisdiction.

## How enforcement of an award gets refused

The grounds are narrow by design, and they are grounds of *procedure and propriety* rather than a re-hearing of the merits. An enforcing court is not permitted to disagree with the tribunal's conclusions.

Broadly, enforcement may be refused where the arbitration agreement was invalid, where a party was denied a proper opportunity to present its case, where the award goes beyond what was submitted to arbitration, where the tribunal was improperly constituted or the procedure departed from what the parties agreed, where the award has been set aside at the seat, where the subject matter is not arbitrable in the enforcing state, or where enforcement would offend that state's public policy.

**Public policy** is the ground most often invoked and the most variable in practice. What it means is genuinely jurisdiction-dependent, and in some places it has been read broadly enough to function as a general discretion.

## Setting aside is not the same as resisting enforcement

Two distinct routes, frequently conflated.

**Setting aside** — annulment — can only be sought in the courts of the seat. Succeed there and the award is destroyed at source, which usually defeats enforcement everywhere.

**Resisting enforcement** happens in the courts where enforcement is sought, and succeeds only in that jurisdiction. An award refused enforcement in one state can still be enforced in another.

This is another reason the seat matters. A seat whose courts annul awards readily gives your counterparty a single forum in which to kill the award entirely.

## Asset location is what actually determines recovery

You enforce where the assets are — not where the counterparty is incorporated, not where the contract was signed, not where the arbitration was seated.

Which turns the dispute clause into a credit question, and the right time to ask it is at signing: **if this goes wrong, where are the assets I could realistically reach?**

A counterparty whose only meaningful assets sit in a jurisdiction that is hostile to enforcement is a credit risk, whatever the dispute clause says. Recognising that at signing leads to a different conversation — about security, guarantees and payment structure — rather than a better-drafted arbitration clause that will not help.

## Sovereign and state-owned counterparties

Relevant to any deal involving ministries of health, state procurement bodies, or state-owned distributors.

There are **two separate immunities**, and this is the distinction that surprises people. Immunity from **jurisdiction** — being brought before a tribunal or court at all. And immunity from **execution** — having assets seized to satisfy an award.

A state that has agreed to arbitrate has generally waived the first. It has not necessarily waived the second. You can obtain a valid, enforceable award and still find that the assets you identified are protected from execution because they serve sovereign rather than commercial functions.

State-owned enterprises are usually separate legal persons and treated accordingly, but the analysis is fact-specific and the outcome is not always the commercial one.

The practical response is an express waiver of immunity from both jurisdiction and execution, identification of commercial assets at the outset, and — more reliably than either — a structure that does not depend on enforcement.

## Structuring so you never have to enforce

The best enforcement strategy is not needing one.

- A **parent guarantee** from an entity incorporated where enforcement is straightforward
- **Letters of credit or bank guarantees** from a bank in a reachable jurisdiction
- **Escrow**, which lesson 12 covered, holding funds outside the counterparty's control
- **Security** over identified assets in a jurisdiction whose courts will give effect to it
- Payment structures that keep money moving toward you rather than accruing as a claim

Each of these converts an enforcement problem into a documentation problem, which is a far better problem to have.

This is the concrete expression of the point lesson 1 opened with: the indemnity package is a commercial instrument. Its value is not what the clause says. It is what you can actually collect.

lessons.title: Building judgment on risk allocation over time

blocks.markdown:
This module began with an observation: most people who negotiate indemnification clauses have never watched one operate.

Seventeen lessons later, that is still true, and no amount of reading fixes it. What reading can do is make the machinery visible enough that you recognise the terms that will matter before you need them.

## The pattern worth carrying away

Across the whole package, attention and consequence are badly correlated.

The **cap** attracts the most negotiation and decides the fewest claims. The **basket type** — one word — routinely moves a recovery by a multiple. The **escrow's exclusivity** sits in a secondary document and can quietly override the cap that was fought over. The **governing law** gets agreed in the final hour and determines how every other clause is read. The **dispute clause** looks like boilerplate and decides whether a win becomes money.

This is not a coincidence. The terms that attract attention are the ones that look like money. The terms that decide outcomes are the ones that look like mechanics.

## What experienced people actually do differently

Not more analysis. Different first questions.

They check the basket type before the cap. They read the escrow agreement, not only the purchase agreement. They read the exclusions in the R&W policy before treating it as protection. They ask where the counterparty's assets are before agreeing a forum. They look for whether notice is a condition precedent. They ask whether the definition of "third-party claim" captures a regulatory action.

None of that is sophisticated. It is a habit of looking at the mechanics first, acquired by having been surprised.

## The weak feedback loop

Here is the real obstacle to building judgment in this area, and it is worth naming plainly.

You will negotiate many indemnity packages and see very few claims. When a claim does arrive it is often years later, handled by someone else, and resolved without anyone reporting back on which negotiated terms actually mattered.

Almost every other professional skill improves through repetition with feedback. This one does not, because the feedback mostly never arrives.

Which means the loop has to be closed deliberately rather than relied on.

## Closing it on purpose

Three practices, in rough order of how much they return.

**Read the indemnity package of every deal you touch**, including the ones you are not negotiating. The variety is the education. Notice which structures recur, which look unusual, and what the unusual ones are protecting against.

**Post-mortem the claims you do see.** When a claim arrives on any deal in your organisation, go back to the agreement and ask which provisions governed the outcome. Not which were most negotiated — which decided it. This is the only direct feedback available and it is routinely wasted.

**Read other people's disputes.** Published awards are scarce, but judgments on commercial indemnity disputes are not, and they are almost entirely about mechanics: whether notice was adequate, whether a basket tipped, whether consequential damages were excluded, whether a settlement breached a consent provision. It is the closest available substitute for having lived through one.

## One last framing

An indemnity is a bet on a counterparty's continued existence, solvency and willingness to pay, made years in advance, under a law you may not have chosen carefully, enforceable in a forum you may not have thought about, secured by an amount someone negotiated in a side document.

Understood that way, the question at the negotiating table stops being *is this clause acceptable* and becomes *what would actually happen*.

That shift is the whole point of the module. Everything else was machinery.
